job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Superintelligence Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
For our explainer ahead of next Thursday's markup, we want to cover the bill's weak spots. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Superintelligence Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Superintelligence Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COVERED AI SYSTEM.—The term "covered AI system" means—
  (A) an artificial intelligence model trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations in a single training run; or
  (B) any artificial intelligence system that the Secretary determines is capable of substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks.
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED FACILITY.—The term "covered facility" means a data center containing more than 50,000 advanced AI chips.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to train, develop, or deploy a covered AI system.
(b) EXISTING SYSTEMS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to a covered AI system whose training began before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) SAFETY EVALUATION.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered facility shall register the facility with the Department of Commerce.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the Department of Commerce a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the computing workloads run at the facility.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that covered AI systems can be developed safely.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
1. **Section 2(1) — “artificial intelligence model” and “artificial intelligence system” are undefined.** The bill offers no test for what counts as AI or where one system ends and another begins, creating uncertainty for model ensembles, fine-tunes, agentic systems, and products containing multiple models.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — The compute threshold lacks a measurement methodology.** The bill does not say whether to count attempted or completed operations, sparse operations, data preprocessing, failed runs, reinforcement learning, fine-tuning, simulations, or other post-training computation.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Single training run” invites artificial division.** A company could structure development as multiple runs, checkpoints, fine-tunes, or separately trained components, each below \(10^{26}\) operations, even if the combined process produces an equally capable system.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — Exactly \(10^{26}\) operations is outside the definition.** Because coverage begins only when compute is “greater than” the threshold, a run using exactly that amount is not covered.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — Compute can be shifted outside training.** The threshold does not address systems that achieve high performance through inference-time computation, retrieval, tool use, ensembles, or other techniques not characterized as training.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — The definition may become obsolete.** The fixed threshold has no adjustment mechanism for algorithmic or hardware advances that could allow superhuman capabilities with substantially less compute.

7. **Section 2(1)(B) — The capability standard is highly indeterminate.** “Substantially exceeding human performance,” “most,” and “cognitive tasks” are undefined, with no specified human baseline, task set, testing conditions, or required margin of superiority.

8. **Section 2(1)(B) — Coverage may depend on how a system is configured or tested.** The text does not say whether capability includes performance with tools, scaffolding, multiple copies, specialized prompting, or extensive inference-time resources.

9. **Section 2(1)(B) — A model may not be covered until the Secretary formally determines that it is.** The wording can be read to require an individualized determination, allowing a highly capable system to operate unless and until the government identifies and evaluates it.

10. **Section 2(1)(B) — The Secretary’s determination process is unspecified.** There are no testing rules, evidentiary standards, deadlines, notice procedures, appeal provisions, or emergency authorities, increasing both enforcement delay and vulnerability to arbitrary-action or due-process challenges.

11. **Sections 2(1)(B) and 6 — “Secretary” is ambiguous.** Section 6 expressly involves the Secretary of State, while the registry belongs to Commerce; the bill never establishes which Secretary makes capability determinations or otherwise administers the Act.

12. **Section 2(2) — The “U.S. person” definition omits many domestic legal persons.** It expressly covers state-chartered corporations but not LLCs, partnerships, trusts, nonprofit associations, federally or territorially chartered entities, or other organizational forms.

13. **Section 2(2) — Foreign subsidiaries and other controlled entities can fall outside extraterritorial coverage.** A U.S. corporation could potentially conduct the prohibited activity through a separately organized foreign subsidiary, because ownership or control by a U.S. person is not addressed.

14. **Section 2(2) — The definition omits some individuals closely tied to the United States.** Permanent residents, U.S. nationals who are not citizens, and other residents are not “U.S. persons,” so the overseas prohibition does not reach them.

15. **Section 2(3) — “Advanced AI chips” is undefined.** Without technical performance criteria or a designated chip list, operators may not know which processors count and could challenge or avoid facility classification.

16. **Section 2(3) — The 50,000-chip threshold is easy to structure around.** Developers could spread chips among several facilities, affiliated operators, campuses, or cloud regions, because the bill contains no aggregation or common-control rule.

17. **Section 2(3) — Exactly 50,000 chips is not covered.** “More than 50,000” excludes a facility containing precisely 50,000 qualifying chips.

18. **Section 2(3) — “Data center,” “containing,” and facility boundaries are unclear.** Operators could dispute whether adjacent buildings, temporarily installed chips, leased equipment, or multiple tenants constitute one covered facility.

19. **Section 3(a) — “Train, develop, or deploy” is undefined.** The bill does not specify whether these terms encompass fine-tuning, modifying, copying, hosting, providing API access, open-source release, internal testing, or integrating an existing model into another product.

20. **Section 3(a) — Important supporting conduct is not expressly prohibited.** Financing, selling chips, supplying cloud services, transferring model weights, publishing technical assistance, possessing a system, and aiding or conspiring with a foreign developer are not independently addressed.

21. **Section 3(a) — Distributed and cross-border projects create jurisdictional gaps.** The bill does not explain when activity occurs “in the United States” if personnel, chips, data, and orchestration are located in different countries.

22. **Section 3(a) — The bill does not say when a compute-based violation begins.** A model is not covered under section 2(1)(A) until a run exceeds the threshold, leaving unclear whether only the threshold-crossing operations are unlawful or whether the entire run is treated as prohibited.

23. **Section 3(b) — The existing-systems exception is an expansive grandfather clause.** Any system whose training “began” before enactment appears exempt not only from continued training but also from the prohibitions on development and deployment, without a completion deadline or capability limit.

24. **Section 3(b) — Token pre-enactment activity may secure an exemption.** Because “began” is undefined, a company could argue that preliminary or minimal training before enactment permanently grandfathered a later, much larger project.

25. **Section 3(b) — Model lineage is unresolved.** The text does not say whether retrained versions, fine-tunes, successor models, merged models, or systems incorporating a grandfathered model remain the same “covered AI system.”

26. **Sections 3(b) and 8 — The delayed effective date creates a six-month grandfathering window.** Section 3(b) uses the date of enactment, but the Act does not take effect for 180 days; firms could begin training during that interval and then claim the exemption once the prohibition becomes operative.

27. **Section 3(c) — The safety-evaluation exception has no objective limits.** It requires no license, government approval, independent oversight, compute cap, security precautions, reporting, or destruction of the resulting system.

28. **Section 3(c) — A stated safety purpose could shield broader development.** The exception turns on “the purpose” of an activity without addressing mixed motives or requiring that the activity be reasonably necessary and narrowly tailored to evaluation.

29. **Section 3(c) — The exception appears to reach deployment as well as training.** Because it exempts “activities” from all of subsection (a), a company could argue that real-world deployment undertaken to evaluate safety is permitted.

30. **Section 4(a) — “Operator” is undefined.** Ownership, day-to-day control, cloud tenancy, and management may be divided among different entities, making responsibility for registration contestable.

31. **Section 4 — Registration duties can be avoided by remaining below the facility threshold.** The registry does not cover distributed clusters or facilities with fewer than 50,001 chips, even when they collectively supply enough compute for a prohibited run.

32. **Section 4 — Registration and reporting requirements are underspecified.** The bill provides no registration deadline, report format, required workload details, record-retention period, audit standard, or rulemaking authority.

33. **Section 4(b) — “Describing the computing workloads” is vague.** A high-level description may technically comply without disclosing customers, compute used, model identity, training dates, or other information needed to detect a violation.

34. **Sections 4 and 5 — Registry violations carry no stated penalty.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3, so failure to register, failure to report, false certification, or an incomplete report is not itself subject to the Act’s civil or criminal penalties.

35. **Sections 4 and 5 — The government receives few investigative or enforcement tools.** The bill supplies no inspection, audit, subpoena, preservation, monitoring, injunction, seizure, or shutdown authority and does not identify an enforcing agency.

36. **Section 5(a) — The civil-enforcement procedure is missing.** The provision does not say who may bring an action, which agency assesses penalties, what process applies, where review occurs, or what limitations period governs.

37. **Section 5(a) — “Each day” is unclear for discrete conduct.** Daily penalties fit continuous deployment but are difficult to apply to a one-time transfer, release, training run, or development decision; the bill does not define when such a violation starts or ends.

38. **Section 5(a) — The civil penalty is only a maximum.** With no minimum, penalty factors, disgorgement, or percentage-of-revenue measure, sanctions could be small relative to the resources and potential gains of major developers.

39. **Section 5(b) — “Willfully” is not defined.** Litigation could center on whether prosecutors must prove only intentional conduct or also knowledge that the conduct was illegal, especially given the Act’s uncertain technical terms.

40. **Sections 5 and 8 — The penalty date conflicts with the effective date.** Section 5 purports to cover violations on or after enactment, while section 8 delays the entire Act for 180 days; this creates uncertainty about liability during the intervening period and invites retroactivity and fair-notice challenges.

41. **Section 6 — The international provision imposes only an effort obligation.** Requiring the Secretary of State to “seek to negotiate” does not require an agreement to be concluded, ratified, implemented, or enforced.

42. **Section 6 — “Equivalent” foreign prohibitions are undefined.** The bill supplies no standard for judging equivalence and no consequence if other countries refuse, allowing prohibited work simply to migrate to nonparticipating jurisdictions.

43. **Section 7(a) — The National Academies report is not actually required.** No provision directs the Academies to prepare it, appropriates funds, specifies its contents, or sets a deadline, so the mechanism for ending the prohibition may never become available.

44. **Section 7(a) — The termination mechanism lacks procedures and a clear operative date.** There is no expedited process for the joint resolution and no express statement of when section 3 ends if such a resolution becomes law.

45. **Section 7(a) — The safety finding is itself vague.** “Can be developed safely” supplies no risk threshold, evidence standard, or definition of safety, making the finding highly contestable.

46. **Section 7 — The two duration provisions are poorly coordinated.** Section 7(a) says the prohibition lasts until a safety finding, but section 7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless of whether such a finding ever occurs.

47. **Section 7(b) — There is no savings clause.** Saying the Act “shall cease to have effect” could generate disputes over pending enforcement actions, unpaid penalties, ongoing prosecutions, reporting records, and liability for pre-sunset conduct.

48. **Act-wide — The bill lacks implementation and transition rules.** It contains no express rulemaking authority, agency assignments, appropriations, treatment of attempts or evasion, whistleblower protections, judicial-review framework, severability clause, or mechanism for updating technical definitions, all of which could impede enforcement or magnify challenges to ambiguous provisions.
